name: Porcelain
what: Hard white ceramic fired at about 1,300 °C from kaolin clay and porcelain stone. For eight centuries only Chinese kilns could make it, and the world called it "china".
why: The first global luxury good. Following it shows the Indian Ocean, the Manila galleons and the Dutch East India Company at work, then centuries of copying (Delft, Arita, Meissen) until Europe cracked the recipe.
now: Mass-made everywhere; Jingdezhen still works as China's porcelain capital.

sources.cite: Finlay, R. (2010). The Pilgrim Art: Cultures of Porcelain in World History. University of California Press.
Gleeson, J. (1998). The Arcanum: The Extraordinary True Story of the Invention of European Porcelain. Bantam.

stops.note: Kilns near Jingdezhen took the town's new name from the Jingde reign (1004) and supplied the court. Local kaolin and porcelain stone, plus pine for the kilns, made it the centre of the world's porcelain for 900 years.
The deep blue of Yuan blue-and-white came from cobalt ore from Persia, probably mined at Qamsar near Kashan, which Chinese potters called "Muslim blue".
Persian cobalt meets Chinese porcelain: blue-and-white is perfected at Jingdezhen in the 1320s-1350s, at first mostly for buyers in the Islamic world.
Quanzhou, Marco Polo's Zaiton and Ibn Battuta's greatest port in the world, shipped porcelain south and west in great junks.
Excavations at Fustat have turned up hundreds of thousands of sherds of Chinese ceramics, and Egyptian potters copied blue-and-white in local earthenware.
Chinese bowls were set into the domes and walls of Kilwa's Great Mosque and Husuni Kubwa palace on the Swahili coast.
Two years after Spain founded Manila, Fujianese junks were selling silk and porcelain there for American silver. The galleons of 1573 are recorded carrying 22,300 pieces of porcelain.
The Manila galleon landed Chinese porcelain at Acapulco; mule trains carried it to Mexico City, where it inspired the blue-and-white Talavera of Puebla.

The Dutch seized the Portuguese carrack Santa Catarina off Singapore in 1603 and auctioned its cargo, including about 100,000 pieces of porcelain, in Amsterdam in 1604. Its thin-walled "kraak" ware started a European craze.
Shah Abbas gave 1,162 pieces of Chinese porcelain to his ancestors' shrine at Ardabil. Over 800 survive, now in the National Museum of Iran.
When the Ming-Qing wars cut supply, Delft potters imitated Chinese blue-and-white in tin-glazed earthenware. Delftware looked like porcelain but was not.
Korean potters brought to Japan after the invasions of the 1590s found porcelain stone at Izumiyama near Arita. With Jingdezhen in chaos, the VOC ordered Arita ware from 1659, shipped from Imari.

Johann Friedrich Böttger, an alchemist held by Augustus the Strong, and Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus made Europe's first true hard-paste porcelain; the Meissen factory opened in 1710 and kept the recipe a state secret.
Under the Canton system (1757-1842) all European trade went through Canton. Workshops there painted Jingdezhen blanks to order, with family crests and European scenes.
The Empress of China, the first American ship to trade with China, came home to New York in May 1785 with tea and porcelain; George Washington bought some.

Staffordshire potters added bone ash to the clay; Josiah Spode II made bone china the English standard around 1800, and cheap transfer-printed "willow pattern" put fake-Chinese blue-and-white on every table.
